concepts.name: Wave optics, the optics of light interacting with small objects
concepts.why: Geometric optics treats light as rays and works whenever light meets objects several times larger than its wavelength. When light meets something small, such as a narrow slit, it shows its wave character instead, and the colors of a soap bubble or an oil slick can only be explained that way. Knowing when the ray picture fails is what tells the reader which kind of optics a problem needs.
concepts.evidence: The book says that light travels in straight lines and acts like a ray when it interacts with objects several times as large as its wavelength, but that when it interacts with smaller objects it displays its wave characteristics prominently. The introduction names the branch of optics that considers these wave characteristics wave optics, and the summary says it must be used whenever light interacts with small objects.

concepts.name: Interference as the most certain indication of a wave
concepts.why: A ray passing through slits would continue straight ahead, while a wave spreads out into bright and dark regions. Seeing that pattern is how we know light is a wave, and the same test applies to water, sound and even matter. Every later section of the chapter reads a pattern of light and dark as evidence of interference.
concepts.evidence: The book says that interference is the hallmark of a wave, and Figure 27.3 shows a laser beam from an observatory acting like a ray beside a beam spread by vertical slits into a pattern of bright and dark regions caused by constructive and destructive interference. A boxed note, Making Connections: Waves, states that the most certain indication of a wave is interference.

concepts.name: The wavelength of light in a medium, λ_n = λ/n
concepts.why: When light enters a medium its speed drops to c/n but its frequency stays fixed, so its wavelength must shrink by the same factor n. Every interference condition in a film or a medium depends on the wavelength there rather than in vacuum, which is why this small result returns in the thin film section.
concepts.evidence: The book divides both sides of $c = f\lambda$ by $n$ to get $v = f\lambda_{n}$, and so $\lambda_{n} = \lambda/n$. It works the range of visible wavelengths in water, 380 to 760 nm becoming 285 to 570 nm, and the problems ask for the wavelength in crown glass and the index of a material from the ratio of its wavelengths.

concepts.name: The frequency and the color of light stay the same in a medium
concepts.why: Light in a medium behaves like a forced oscillation that keeps the frequency of its source. Its speed and wavelength change, but its color does not, because color is associated with frequency. This keeps the reader from supposing that red light turns blue when it enters water.
concepts.evidence: The book says that when light goes from a vacuum to some medium, its speed and wavelength change but its frequency remains the same, and that although wavelengths change while traveling from one medium to another, colors do not, since colors are associated with frequency.

concepts.name: Huygens’s principle: every point on a wavefront is a source of wavelets
concepts.why: Huygens’s principle is a technique for finding where a wave goes next. Every point on a wavefront sends out a wavelet that spreads forward at the wave's speed, and the new wavefront is the line tangent to all of them. It explains reflection, refraction and diffraction with one construction, and the rest of the chapter uses it to find how light from slits interferes.
concepts.evidence: The book states the principle in italics and applies it to a straight wavefront in Figure 27.5, where each point emits a semicircular wavelet that moves a distance $s = vt$ and the new wavefront is a line tangent to the wavelets. The AP item asks which statement about the principle is true, with the key that each point on a wavefront can be considered a new wave source.

concepts.name: Huygens’s principle explains the laws of reflection and refraction
concepts.why: The laws of reflection and refraction were stated for rays in the previous chapter. Huygens’s construction shows why they hold: wavelets from a mirror leave in turn and build a wavefront at an angle equal to the incident one, and wavelets in a slower medium travel less far, so the wavefront turns toward the perpendicular.
concepts.evidence: Figure 27.6 applies the principle to a wavefront striking a mirror and shows the new wavefront reflected at an angle equal to the incident angle. Figure 27.7 applies it to a wavefront passing into a medium where its speed is less, and the book says this explains why a ray changes direction to become closer to the perpendicular when light slows down.

concepts.name: Diffraction, the bending of a wave around an opening or obstacle
concepts.why: Sound fills a room through an open door, while light casts a sharp shadow of the doorway. Both are waves, and the difference is the ratio of the wavelength to the opening. Diffraction is the bending of a wave around edges, and seeing it is evidence that something is a wave; this is the idea that the slit sections of the chapter make quantitative.
concepts.evidence: The book defines diffraction as the bending of a wave around the edges of an opening or an obstacle and says that if diffraction is observed for some phenomenon, it is evidence that the phenomenon is a wave. Figure 27.8 contrasts light passing through a doorway with sound, whose wavelength of about 0.33 m is similar to the size of the door.

concepts.name: Diffraction is greatest for openings about the size of the wavelength
concepts.why: How much a wave bends depends on the size of the opening compared with its wavelength. A wide opening lets the wavefront through almost straight, and a narrow one spreads it widely. This is the reason light behaves like a ray in everyday life and like a wave in a narrow slit.
concepts.evidence: Figure 27.9 applies Huygens’s principle to wavefronts striking openings of decreasing size, and its caption says the amount of bending is more extreme for a small opening, consistent with the fact that wave characteristics are most noticeable for interactions with objects about the same size as the wavelength. The conceptual questions ask why sound bends around a building while light does not.

concepts.name: Coherent and incoherent light
concepts.why: Two waves only produce a steady pattern of interference if they keep a definite phase relationship. Young passed sunlight through a single slit first to make it somewhat coherent, and the double slit then gave two coherent sources. Two headlights of a car, whose phases are random, produce no such pattern.
concepts.evidence: The book defines coherent as waves that are in phase or have a definite phase relationship and incoherent as waves with random phase relationships, and says that two slits provide two coherent light sources that then interfere constructively or destructively. A conceptual question asks whether two independent sources such as headlights would give the same pattern.

concepts.name: Young’s double slit experiment shows that light is a wave
concepts.why: Newton's view that light was not a wave prevailed until Young, in 1801, sent light through two narrow slits and found a pattern of many bright and dark lines rather than two lines. Waves from the two slits overlap and interfere, and this experiment gave definitive proof of the wave character of light.
concepts.evidence: The book says the acceptance of the wave character of light came when Thomas Young did his double slit experiment, shown in Figure 27.10, and that without diffraction and interference the light would simply make two lines on the screen. The summary states that Young’s double slit experiment gave definitive proof of the wave character of light.

concepts.name: The path length difference from two slits, Δl = d sin θ
concepts.why: Whether two waves arrive in phase depends on how much farther one has travelled. For a distant screen the two paths are nearly parallel, and simple trigonometry gives their difference as d sin θ. This single expression is the heart of every slit and grating result in the chapter.
concepts.evidence: Figure 27.14 shows the two paths from the slits to a common point on the screen, and the book says simple trigonometry shows the difference between them to be $d\sin\theta$, assuming the distance to the screen is much greater than the distance between slits. Figure 27.13 shows that a path half a wavelength longer gives a dark spot and one a whole wavelength longer gives a bright one.

concepts.name: Constructive interference for a double slit, d sin θ = mλ
concepts.why: Bright fringes appear where the paths differ by a whole number of wavelengths. The condition tells the reader where every bright line on the screen lies, and it shows that the smaller the slit separation, the larger the angle, which is the chapter's rule that wave effects grow when the object is small.
concepts.evidence: The book states that to obtain constructive interference the path length difference must be an integral multiple of the wavelength, $d\sin\theta = m\lambda$ for $m = 0, 1, -1, 2, -2, \ldots$, and notes that for fixed $\lambda$ and $m$ the smaller $d$ is, the larger $\theta$ must be. Example 27.1 and most of the section's problems use it.

concepts.name: Destructive interference for a double slit, d sin θ = (m + ½)λ
concepts.why: Dark fringes appear where the paths differ by a half-integral number of wavelengths, so crest meets trough. With the bright condition it completes the pattern of alternating fringes and lets the reader find the angle of any minimum.
concepts.evidence: The book states that to obtain destructive interference the path length difference must be a half-integral multiple of the wavelength, $d\sin\theta = (m + \frac{1}{2})\lambda$, and the problems ask for the slit separation or the wavelength from the angle of a first or third minimum.

concepts.name: The order m of an interference fringe
concepts.why: Each bright fringe is labelled by the integer m, the number of whole wavelengths by which its two paths differ. Counting from the central fringe, which is order zero, is how the reader names a fringe in a problem such as the third bright line.
concepts.evidence: The book calls $m$ the order of the interference and gives the example that $m = 4$ is fourth-order interference. Example 27.1 reads the third bright line as third-order constructive interference, $m = 3$.

concepts.name: Finding a wavelength or a slit separation from a double slit pattern
concepts.why: Interference patterns can be used to measure wavelength, which is how Young measured visible wavelengths and how spectra are still measured. The reader solves d sin θ = mλ for whichever quantity is unknown.
concepts.evidence: Example 27.1 finds the wavelength of a He-Ne laser, 633 nm, from the angle of the third bright line through slits 0.0100 mm apart, and its discussion says interference patterns can be used to measure wavelength. The problems ask for angles, separations and wavelengths from both conditions.

concepts.name: Finding the highest order of interference possible
concepts.why: A pattern does not have an infinite number of lines, because sin θ can be no larger than 1. Setting sin θ = 1 gives the largest order that reaches the screen, and it shows why widely spaced slits give many fringes.
concepts.evidence: Example 27.2 solves $d\sin\theta = m\lambda$ for $m$ with $\sin\theta = 1$ and finds that the largest integer $m$ can be is 15 for the slits of the preceding example. The problems ask for the highest-order maximum and the largest wavelength that gives a first-order maximum.

concepts.name: The spacing of fringes on a distant screen, Δy = xλ/d
concepts.why: For small angles the fringes of a double slit are evenly spaced on the screen, and their spacing grows with the distance to the screen and the wavelength and shrinks with the slit separation. It is how a measured distance on a screen becomes a wavelength.
concepts.evidence: A problem of the section shows that for small angles the distance between fringes is $\Delta y = x\lambda/d$, and the figure beside it marks $x$, $y$ and $\Delta y$. Two later problems use the result to find a fringe spacing and a wavelength.

concepts.name: A diffraction grating, many evenly spaced parallel slits
concepts.why: A diffraction grating forms a pattern very much like a double slit's, with bright regions at the same angles, but with many more slits. Gratings work by transmission and by reflection, and they occur in nature in opals, butterfly wings and bird feathers, whose colors come from interference rather than pigment.
concepts.evidence: The book defines a diffraction grating as a large number of evenly spaced parallel slits and says the interference pattern it creates is very similar to the one formed by a double slit, as Figure 27.16 shows. Figure 27.17 shows an opal and butterfly wings acting as reflection gratings, and the book calls the effect in feathers iridescence.

concepts.name: Constructive interference for a grating, d sin θ = mλ
concepts.why: Each ray from a grating travels d sin θ farther than its neighbor, so all of them arrive in phase when that distance is a whole number of wavelengths. The condition is exactly the double slit's, which the reader can carry over directly; the slits of a grating are simply closer, giving fewer maxima at larger angles.
concepts.evidence: Figure 27.19 shows rays from each slit traveling in the same direction, each a distance $d\sin\theta$ farther than its neighbor, and the book states the condition $d\sin\theta = m\lambda$ and notes that this is exactly the same equation as for double slits separated by $d$.

concepts.name: A grating's maxima are narrower and brighter than a double slit's
concepts.why: What makes a grating useful is that its bright regions are narrower and brighter and its dark regions darker than a double slit's. The more slits there are, the sharper the maxima, which is why a grating can separate wavelengths that lie close together.
concepts.evidence: The book says gratings form a sharper pattern than double slits do, and Figure 27.18 shows idealized graphs in which the maxima of the grating are at the same angles as the double slit's but narrower, and its caption says the maxima become narrower as the number of slits is increased.

concepts.name: Finding the angles and screen positions of a grating's spectrum
concepts.why: White light through a grating is spread into a rainbow in every order except the central one, with violet nearest the center. Finding the angle of each wavelength from d sin θ = mλ and then its position from y = x tan θ is how a grating becomes a spectroscopic tool.
concepts.evidence: Example 27.3 finds the first-order angles of 380-nm and 760-nm light through a grating with 10,000 lines per centimeter, 22.33° and 49.46°, and then the positions on a screen 2.00 m away, which differ by 1.52 m. Figure 27.16(b) shows the white central maximum and the rainbows of the higher orders.

concepts.name: The single slit diffraction pattern and its broad central maximum
concepts.why: Light from different parts of one slit interferes with itself. The result is a pattern whose central maximum is wider and much brighter than the dimmer maxima on either side, quite unlike the evenly spaced lines of a grating. The narrower the slit, the more the pattern spreads.
concepts.evidence: Figure 27.21 shows the single slit pattern, and the book notes that the central maximum is larger than those on either side and that the intensity decreases rapidly on either side. Figure 27.23 graphs the intensity and says the central maximum is six times higher than shown. The conceptual question asks how the pattern changes as the slit is narrowed.

concepts.name: Destructive interference for a single slit, D sin θ = mλ
concepts.why: When the rays from the top and bottom of the slit differ in path by one wavelength, each ray from one half of the slit has a partner from the other half that cancels it, and a minimum appears. Minima fall where D sin θ is a whole number of wavelengths, and there is no minimum of order zero.
concepts.evidence: Figure 27.22 shows the ray bundle at four angles and explains that a ray from the center travels $\lambda/2$ farther than one from the edge and interferes destructively. The book states $D\sin\theta = m\lambda$ for $m = 1, -1, 2, -2, 3, \ldots$ and the summary notes that there is no $m = 0$ minimum.

concepts.name: Finding a slit width, a wavelength or the angle of a minimum
concepts.why: Solving D sin θ = mλ gives the width of a slit from the angle of one of its minima, or the angle of any other minimum once the width is known. The same condition applies to sound through a door and ocean waves through a harbor opening.
concepts.evidence: Example 27.4 finds the width of a slit, $1.56\times10^{-6}$ m, from a second minimum at 45.0° for 550-nm light and then the first minimum at 20.7°, and its discussion finds the second maximum about half as wide as the central one. The problems include a harbor and a hangar door as single slits.

concepts.name: Diffraction limits the detail an image can show
concepts.why: Light through a circular aperture spreads into a fuzzy spot surrounded by rings, and the images of two close point sources overlap. Every lens, mirror and pupil has a finite diameter, so this limit to resolution is an inescapable consequence of the wave nature of light.
concepts.evidence: Figure 27.25 shows the diffraction pattern of a small circular aperture and two point sources that can just be distinguished and then cannot. The book says diffraction limits the resolution of any system having a lens or mirror, and the AP item asks how the width of the central maximum depends on the size of the aperture.

concepts.name: The Rayleigh criterion, θ = 1.22 λ/D
concepts.why: Two images are just resolvable when the center of one diffraction pattern lies on the first minimum of the other, which for a circular aperture occurs at θ = 1.22 λ/D in radians. A larger aperture or a shorter wavelength resolves finer detail, which is why the Hubble telescope sees so much and why Arecibo, for all its size, does not.
concepts.evidence: The book states the Rayleigh criterion in italics, gives the angle $\theta = 1.22\lambda/D$, and shows it in Figure 27.26. Example 27.5 finds $2.80\times10^{-7}$ rad for the Hubble Space Telescope's 2.40-m mirror, and Figure 27.28's caption compares Arecibo's poorer limit at radio wavelengths.

concepts.name: Finding the smallest resolvable separation at a distance, s = rθ
concepts.why: Once the smallest resolvable angle is known, the distance between two objects that can just be told apart is that angle times their distance away. This turns the Rayleigh criterion into answers about stars in Andromeda, craters on the Moon or headlights on a road.
concepts.evidence: Example 27.5(b) uses $s = r\theta$ to find that two stars 2 million light years away can be resolved if they are about 0.56 ly apart. The problems ask for the smallest detail on the Moon, the distance at which headlights can be resolved and the spot a laser makes on the Moon.

concepts.name: Every beam of finite diameter spreads by diffraction
concepts.why: Even a beam of rays made as parallel as possible spreads out at an angle of about 1.22 λ/D because its diameter is limited. The spreading can be reduced only by making the beam wider, which is why a laser sent to the Moon is first expanded through a telescope.
concepts.evidence: The book says any beam of light having a finite diameter $D$ and a wavelength $\lambda$ exhibits diffraction spreading at an angle $\theta = 1.22\lambda/D$, and Figure 27.29 shows the spreading from a microwave antenna. The conceptual question asks why lenses, mirrors or apertures cannot correct the spreading.

concepts.name: The resolving power of a lens, x = 1.22 λd/D
concepts.why: In a microscope what matters is not an angle but the smallest distance between two points that can still be seen as distinct. The Rayleigh angle with the small angle approximation gives that distance, and the smaller it is, the greater the resolution.
concepts.evidence: The book defines the resolving power of a lens as the smallest distance $x$ by which two objects can be separated and still be seen as distinct, sets $\theta = 1.22\lambda/D = x/d$ for the arrangement of Figure 27.30(a), and obtains $x = 1.22\lambda d/D$.

concepts.name: Numerical aperture and the resolution of a microscope objective
concepts.why: The numerical aperture NA = n sin α measures how wide a cone of light a lens can gather. A lens with a larger NA collects more light, gives a brighter image and resolves finer detail, and its resolving power is 0.61 λn/NA. It also makes the focal spot smaller, which in wave optics is never a true point.
concepts.evidence: Figure 27.30(b) shows the acceptance angle of a microscope objective, and the book writes $\text{NA} = n\sin\alpha$ and $x = 0.61\lambda n/\text{NA}$, saying a lens with a large NA will be able to resolve finer details. Figure 27.31 contrasts the geometric focal point with the extended focal region of wave optics, whose size decreases with increasing NA.

concepts.name: Thin film interference between light reflected from two surfaces
concepts.why: The colors of a soap bubble and an oil slick come from light reflected from the top and bottom surfaces of a thin film. The ray that enters the film travels farther and may return in or out of phase with the ray reflected at the top, so different thicknesses favor different colors.
concepts.evidence: Figure 27.33 shows ray 1 reflected from the top surface of a film and ray 2 reflected from the bottom, and the book says these rays interfere in a way that depends on the thickness of the film and the indices of refraction of the media. The AP item asks for the cause of thin film interference, with the key that it is light reflecting from the top and bottom surfaces of a film.

concepts.name: A half-wavelength shift on reflection from a medium of higher index
concepts.why: A soap bubble is dark where it is thinnest, although the paths there are almost equal. The reason is that light reflecting from a medium with a greater index of refraction than the one it travels in gains a 180° phase change, a λ/2 shift. Deciding at which surfaces this happens is the first step of every thin film problem.
concepts.evidence: The book states the rule in italics: when light reflects from a medium having an index of refraction greater than that of the medium in which it is traveling, a 180° phase change, or a $\lambda/2$ shift, occurs. It applies the rule to a soap bubble, where there is a shift for ray 1 and none for ray 2, and the conceptual questions ask at which surfaces of a contact lens or a cover glass the shift occurs.

concepts.name: Deciding whether a film interferes constructively or destructively
concepts.why: For light incident perpendicularly the second ray travels about 2t farther, measured in wavelengths in the film. The reader combines that path difference with the phase changes at the two surfaces: a total shift of a whole number of wavelengths is constructive and a half-integral number is destructive.
concepts.evidence: The book writes $2t = \lambda_{n}, 2\lambda_{n}, 3\lambda_{n}, \ldots$ and $2t = \lambda_{n}/2, 3\lambda_{n}/2, 5\lambda_{n}/2, \ldots$ and says one must also determine whether there is a phase change upon reflection. Example 27.7 finds the thicknesses of a soap bubble that reflect 650-nm light constructively, 122, 366 and 610 nm, and destructively, 0, 244 and 488 nm.

concepts.name: Designing a non-reflective coating
concepts.why: A thin layer on a lens can make the light reflected from its two surfaces cancel. When both reflections carry a phase change, the thinnest such coating is a quarter of the wavelength in the film thick. Blodgett's non-reflective glass is this idea, and cameras, microscopes and sunglasses rely on it.
concepts.evidence: Example 27.6 finds that a magnesium fluoride coating of index 1.38 on glass of index 1.52 must be at least 99.6 nm thick to limit the reflection of 550-nm light, since both rays have a $\lambda/2$ shift and ray 2 must travel a half wavelength farther. The book describes Blodgett's patent of non-reflective glass in 1938.

concepts.name: Air wedges and Newton’s rings as fringes of equal thickness
concepts.why: A film whose thickness changes steadily shows a band of color, or of light and dark in pure light, for every step of one wavelength. Two microscope slides with a hair between them, or a lens pressed on a flat blank, show these bands, which lets a lens be ground to an accuracy of less than a wavelength.
concepts.evidence: Figure 27.34 shows the rainbow bands in the wedge of air between two microscope slides, with a dark band where they touch, and Figure 27.35 shows Newton’s rings. The book says each successive ring of a given color indicates an increase of only one wavelength in the distance between the lens and the blank. Two problems find the band spacing and the thickness of debris under a slide.

concepts.name: Polarization, the direction of a transverse wave's oscillations
concepts.why: Light is a transverse wave whose electric and magnetic fields oscillate perpendicular to its direction of travel. Polarization is the attribute that these oscillations have a definite direction, and for light the direction of polarization is defined to be the direction of the electric field. Only a transverse wave can be polarized.
concepts.evidence: The book defines polarization as the attribute that a wave’s oscillations have a definite direction relative to the direction of propagation, and defines the direction of polarization of an EM wave as the direction parallel to the electric field, as Figure 27.37 shows. Figure 27.38 compares vertically and horizontally polarized waves on ropes passing a vertical slit, and the AP item asks for the direction of polarization.

concepts.name: Unpolarized light and polarizing filters
concepts.why: The Sun and most other sources produce unpolarized light, made of waves with every direction of polarization. A polarizing filter acts as a slit, passing only the electric field parallel to its axis, so light leaving it is polarized. Two crossed filters pass nothing at all.
concepts.evidence: The book says light that is composed of many waves with all possible directions of polarization is unpolarized, and that the axis of a polarizing filter is the direction along which it passes the electric field, as Figures 27.39 and 27.40 show. Figure 27.41 shows that when the axes of two filters are perpendicular, no light is passed by the second.

concepts.name: Malus’s law, I = I₀ cos² θ
concepts.why: A filter passes only the component E cos θ of a polarized wave's field, and since intensity goes as the square of the amplitude, the transmitted intensity is I₀ cos² θ. It tells the reader how bright light is after any number of filters, and why a third filter placed between two crossed ones lets light through.
concepts.evidence: The book says the transmitted part of the wave has an amplitude $E\cos\theta$, shown in Figure 27.42, and that the intensity is $I = I_{0}\cos^{2}\theta$, known as Malus’s law. Example 27.8 finds that an angle of 71.6° reduces the intensity by 90.0%, and the problems use the law for two and three filters.

concepts.name: Reflected light is partly polarized
concepts.why: Polaroid sunglasses cut glare because light reflected from water or glass is left more horizontally polarized, while the vertically polarized part is preferentially refracted. Sunglasses with vertical axes therefore block more reflected light than light from other sources.
concepts.evidence: Figure 27.36 shows a river photographed with and without a polarizing filter, and Figure 27.43 shows unpolarized light reflected from a surface as partially polarized light. The book says the reflected light is left more horizontally polarized and offers the mnemonic of arrows bouncing on their sides.

concepts.name: Brewster’s law, tan θ_b = n₂/n₁
concepts.why: At one angle of reflection, Brewster’s angle, the reflected light is completely polarized. It depends only on the two indices of refraction, which is why sunglasses work about equally well on water and on glass.
concepts.evidence: The book states that reflected light is completely polarized at an angle of reflection $\theta_{\text{b}}$ given by $\tan\theta_{\text{b}} = n_{2}/n_{1}$, known as Brewster’s law. Example 27.9 finds Brewster’s angle as 53.1° for water and 56.7° for crown glass, and the problems ask for it from diamond, water and a gemstone.

concepts.name: Light scattered by air is polarized
concepts.why: Sunlight shakes the electrons of air molecules perpendicular to its direction of travel, and they radiate like small antennae. Light scattered at right angles to the original ray is therefore polarized, which is why the blue sky grows bright and dim through rotating sunglasses and why photographers darken the sky with a filter.
concepts.evidence: Figure 27.46 shows unpolarized sunlight scattering from a molecule, with polarized light leaving at right angles and partially polarized light in other directions. The book says there can be no polarization in the scattered light parallel to the original ray, because that would require the original ray to be a longitudinal wave.

concepts.name: Liquid crystals, optical activity and birefringence
concepts.why: Some materials act on the direction of polarization itself. A liquid crystal rotates it by 90° unless a voltage is applied, which is how every pixel of an LCD works; optically active substances such as sugar water rotate it by an amount that measures their concentration; stressed plastic shows colored patterns between crossed filters; and a birefringent crystal splits a beam in two.
concepts.evidence: Figure 27.47 shows an LCD pixel passing light with no voltage and blocking it with voltage on. The book defines optically active substances as those that rotate the plane of polarization, shown with an analyzer in Figure 27.48, shows optical stress analysis in Figure 27.49, and defines birefringent crystals as those that split an unpolarized beam into two, as calcite does in Figure 27.50.

concepts.name: The wavelength limits the detail a microscope can show
concepts.why: Because light diffracts around small objects, details much smaller than its wavelength cannot be seen, just as radar cannot see the rivets of an aircraft. Shorter wavelengths, as in ultraviolet microscopes, show somewhat finer detail but bring their own drawbacks.
concepts.evidence: The book says one rule of thumb has it that all details smaller than about $\lambda$ are difficult to observe, that visible light cannot detect individual atoms since atoms are about 0.1 nm in size, and that ultraviolet microscopes allow somewhat greater detail but are severely limited by the hazard of UV to living tissue.

concepts.name: Interference and phase-contrast microscopes enhance contrast
concepts.why: Many microscopic objects absorb little light, so they barely stand out from the background. Light passing through an object of different index emerges out of phase with light from the background, and superimposing the two makes the difference visible as contrast. Interference, phase-contrast and polarization microscopes all use a wave property of light in this way.
concepts.evidence: The book defines contrast as the difference in intensity between objects and the background and says that light emerging from the object is out of phase with light from the background, as Figure 27.51 shows. Figures 27.52 and 27.53 show the interference microscope's object and reference beams and the phase plate of the phase-contrast microscope.

concepts.name: Confocal microscopes use the extended focal region to image in three dimensions
concepts.why: A confocal microscope uses the extended focal region of wave optics and a pinhole that blocks light from points out of focus. Scanning the pinhole sideways and then up and down builds a three-dimensional image of a thick specimen, even of live cells in motion.
concepts.evidence: Figure 27.54 shows the laser, the dichroic mirror, the two pinholes and the detector, and its caption says that in-focus rays pass the second pinhole while out-of-focus rays are blocked, and that the result is a three-dimensional image of the specimen. The book notes that the method uses the extended focal region of Figure 27.31(b).
